name: read
synopsis: ssize_t read(int fd, void buf[.count], size_t count);
description: The read() system call attempts to read up to count bytes from the file descriptor fd into the buffer starting at buf. On files that support seeking, it starts at the file offset and increments the offset by the number of bytes read. If the file offset is at or past the end of the file, it returns zero.

parameters.name: fd
parameters.description: File descriptor from which to read

parameters.name: buf
parameters.description: Buffer to store the read data (must be large enough to hold up to count bytes)

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Maximum number of bytes to read

return_value.success: Returns the number of bytes read (zero indicates end of file), and advances the file position by this number
return_value.failure: Returns -1 on error, and errno is set to indicate the error; the file position may or may not change

errors.description: The file descriptor fd refers to a file other than a socket and has been marked nonblocking, and the read would block
The file descriptor fd refers to a socket and has been marked nonblocking, and the read would block
fd is not a valid file descriptor or is not open for reading
buf is outside the accessible address space
The call was interrupted by a signal before any data was read
fd is attached to an object unsuitable for reading, or the file was opened with O_DIRECT and alignment issues exist

bugs: Before Linux 3.14, read operations were not atomic with respect to updating the file offset in multi-threaded or multi-process scenarios sharing an open file description.
